A parameter the control unit reports that this app has no decoder for. The raw value is shown as the car sent it, without a formula or a unit behind it. Treat it as a curiosity rather than a diagnosis.

The difference between pressure in the intake manifold and the air pressure outside, so it shows how much the turbo or supercharger is actually adding. On a naturally aspirated engine it stays at or below zero, because the throttle can only ever restrict. It is computed here from manifold and barometric pressure, not read as its own sensor.

How much fuel the engine is burning right now, in litres per hour. Most cars do not report it directly, so it is usually estimated from air flow and the mixture — good enough to compare driving styles, not to settle an argument about the tank. At idle a small petrol engine sits near 0.5–1.5 L/h.

Instantaneous consumption: the current fuel rate divided by the current speed. It swings wildly by design — it goes to infinity when the car stops and near zero when coasting in gear — so it is read as a trend over a few seconds, not as a single number. For an average over a drive, use the trip summary instead.

Voltage measured by the adapter itself at the OBD socket, not by the car. With the engine off it is the resting battery, typically 12.4–12.7 V; with the engine running it is the charging system, typically 13.8–14.6 V. A resting reading under about 12.2 V suggests a discharged or tired battery, and a running reading that stays near 12 V suggests the alternator is not charging.

How hard the engine is working, as a percentage of the torque it could make at these revs. The ECU calculates it from air flow, so it is not a throttle position: cruising gently sits around 20–40 per cent, and full throttle approaches 100 per cent. It is the figure most fuel and ignition maps are indexed on.

Temperature of the coolant leaving the engine, measured at the cylinder head. After warm-up a modern engine holds 80–100 °C and the thermostat keeps it there; brief rises when climbing or sitting in traffic are normal. A reading that stays low suggests a stuck-open thermostat, and one climbing well past 105 °C is worth stopping for.

The instant correction the ECU is applying to the fuel it injects, in percent, based on what the oxygen sensor sees right now. It flickers constantly by design — that flicker is closed-loop control working. Sustained values beyond about ±10 per cent mean the base fuelling is off and the ECU is compensating.

The long-term correction the ECU has learned and stored for the fuel map, in percent. It moves slowly and survives a restart, so it is the honest summary of how far off the base fuelling has drifted. Sustained values beyond about ±10 per cent usually point to a vacuum leak, a fuel delivery problem or a drifting mass air flow sensor.

The same instant fuel correction as bank 1, but for the second bank of cylinders — only engines with two cylinder heads, such as a V6 or a flat four, report it. A large and persistent difference between the two banks is more informative than either number alone, because it points at something on one side only.

The learned, stored fuel correction for the second bank of cylinders. Read it next to bank 1: both drifting the same way suggests something common to the whole engine, such as air metering or fuel pressure, while one bank alone suggests an injector, a leak or a sensor on that side.

Pressure in the low-pressure fuel line, referenced to the intake manifold. It matters most on port-injected engines, where a weak pump or a clogged filter shows up here as pressure that sags under load. Direct-injection engines usually report the far higher rail pressure separately.

Absolute pressure in the intake manifold, measured against vacuum rather than against the air outside. At idle it sits well below atmospheric — roughly 25–45 kPa — because the closed throttle is holding a vacuum, and at full throttle it approaches the outside air pressure, or exceeds it on a boosted engine. This is not boost: for that, the barometric reading has to be subtracted.

Crankshaft speed in revolutions per minute, reported by the ECU from the crank sensor. A warm petrol engine idles around 600–900 rpm, and a cold one deliberately higher for the first minute or two. An idle that wanders or hunts is usually an air leak, a dirty throttle body or an idle control problem.

Road speed as the car itself measures it, from the wheel or gearbox sensors — not from GPS. It is usually a little optimistic by design, since manufacturers must never under-read, so it can sit a few percent above a satellite reading. Fitting non-standard tyre sizes shifts it further.

How many crankshaft degrees before top dead centre the spark fires. The ECU advances it for efficiency and pulls it back when it detects knock or when the engine is under heavy load, so a figure that drops sharply under acceleration is the knock control doing its job. Light cruise typically shows a lot of advance, 25–40°.

Temperature of the air entering the engine, measured in the intake tract. It tracks the outside air on the move and climbs when the car stands still and heat soaks into the intake. Colder air is denser, so this figure feeds directly into how much fuel the ECU decides to inject.

Mass of air entering the engine, in grams per second, straight from the air flow sensor. It is the primary input for how much fuel to inject, so a sensor drifting low makes the whole engine run lean. A healthy small petrol engine reads roughly 2–5 g/s at idle and tens of grams at full throttle.

How far the throttle plate is open, read at the plate itself rather than at the pedal. On a drive-by-wire car the ECU moves the plate, so this does not have to follow the pedal — it idles at a few percent and can open on its own during warm-up or with the air conditioning on.

Seconds since the engine last started, counted by the ECU. It resets on every start, which makes it useful for telling whether a reading has had time to stabilise — coolant temperature, fuel trims and readiness monitors all mean more after a few minutes than after ten seconds.

Distance driven since the check engine light came on. It stays at zero on a healthy car and keeps counting while a fault is active, so a large number means a fault has been ignored for a long time. Clearing the codes resets it.

Fuel rail pressure measured relative to the intake manifold, so it reflects the pressure difference the injectors actually work against. Port injection systems typically hold a few hundred kPa here and should keep it steady as load changes.

Fuel pressure at the injectors measured against a vacuum reference, which is how direct-injection systems report their high-pressure side. Values in the thousands of kPa are normal there; the ECU raises pressure with load and a rail that cannot follow the demand usually shows up as a fuel-pressure fault code.

How far the ECU has asked the exhaust gas recirculation valve to open, as a percentage. It is a command, not a measurement of the valve — the valve can be commanded open and be stuck shut with soot. EGR is normally closed at idle and under full throttle, and opens during light cruise.

The gap between the EGR opening the ECU asked for and the position it actually sees, as a percentage of the demand. Near zero means the valve is following orders; a persistently large error is the classic signature of a valve clogged with carbon or a failing position sensor.

How far the ECU has opened the purge valve that draws petrol vapour from the charcoal canister into the engine. It is a command rather than a flow measurement. Purging normally happens under light cruise with a warm engine, and a valve stuck open can upset the mixture at idle.

How full the tank is, as a percentage, from the same float sender that drives the dashboard gauge. It is coarse and it sloshes: expect it to move in steps and to read differently on a slope. Use it for trends, not for calculating exactly how many litres are left.

How many complete warm-up cycles the engine has done since the fault codes were last cleared. A warm-up cycle means the coolant rose far enough above its starting temperature, so this is the counter that decides when old codes and readiness monitors finally age out. Low numbers after a clear are normal.

Distance driven since the fault codes were last cleared. It is the honest answer to \"how long has this car been driven since somebody reset it\" — a car with a freshly cleared memory and only a few kilometres on this counter has not yet had a chance to prove anything.

Pressure inside the sealed fuel vapour system, measured against the air outside and reported in pascals. The ECU uses it to test the system for leaks, which is what the evaporative monitor does. Small swings with temperature are normal; a system that will not hold any pressure difference points at a loose fuel cap or a cracked hose.

Air pressure around the car, in kilopascals. It sits near 101 kPa at sea level and falls with altitude — roughly 90 kPa at a thousand metres. The ECU needs it to know how much oxygen the air actually holds, and this app subtracts it from manifold pressure to get boost.

Temperature inside the catalytic converter on bank 1, at the first sensor position. A working converter runs hot — several hundred degrees once lit off — because oxidising what the engine did not burn releases heat. Unusually high readings can mean fuel is being burned in the converter rather than in the cylinder.

The same catalyst temperature for bank 2, on engines with two cylinder banks and two converters. Comparing the two banks is the useful part: a large steady difference points at one side running differently from the other.

Catalyst temperature at the second sensor position on bank 1, further downstream than the first. Read together with the upstream figure it shows how much heat the converter is generating along its length.
Catalyst temperature at the second sensor position on bank 2. Only engines with two banks report it, and it is most useful next to the matching bank 1 reading.

Supply voltage as the engine control unit measures it at its own connector. It is close to the adapter\'s socket reading but not identical, because it has the car\'s wiring between it and the battery. A running engine should show the charging system here, typically 13.5–14.6 V.

Cylinder filling relative to a normalised reference, which is why it can exceed 100 per cent on a boosted engine while calculated load cannot. It is the better number for comparing how hard the engine is breathing across different revs, because it does not scale itself to what is possible at the moment.

The air-fuel mixture the ECU has asked for, expressed as lambda where 1.000 is the chemically ideal ratio. This is a command, not a measurement: it says what the ECU wants, while the wide-range sensor says what it got. In closed loop it sits at 1.000 and it goes rich under full throttle.

Throttle opening expressed against the closed position the ECU has learned, so it starts from zero when your foot is off the pedal. It is easier to read than the absolute figure, which never quite reaches zero because the sensor has an offset.

Outside air temperature as the car measures it, usually from a sensor behind the bumper. It lags reality when the car has been standing in the sun and settles once moving. The ECU uses it for climate control and for density corrections.

The reading from the second throttle position sensor. Drive-by-wire throttles carry two sensors that must agree, and the ECU compares them constantly — a disagreement between them is what triggers limp mode rather than either value on its own.
The reading from a third throttle position sensor, on the systems that fit one. Like the other channels it exists for cross-checking rather than for driving anything directly.

How far the accelerator pedal is pressed, from the first of its sensors. On a drive-by-wire car this is your input and the throttle plate position is the ECU\'s response to it, so the two can differ legitimately.
The second accelerator pedal sensor. The pair exists for safety: the ECU only accepts a pedal request that both sensors agree on, and a mismatch is what puts the car into reduced power.
A third accelerator pedal sensor, where one is fitted. It serves the same cross-checking role as the other two channels.

The throttle opening the ECU has commanded the actuator to take, as opposed to the position the plate reports. Comparing the two is a direct check on whether the throttle body is doing what it is told.
How many minutes the engine has run with the check engine light on. Together with the distance counter it separates a fault that appeared on the last trip from one that has been lit for months.

Engine running time since the fault codes were last cleared. Readiness monitors need a certain amount of running to complete, so a small figure here explains why a car is not yet ready for an emissions test.

What the ECU believes it is burning — petrol, diesel, LPG and so on — as a coded value. It is a declaration from the control unit rather than a measurement, and this app uses it to pick the right constants when estimating fuel rate from air flow.

How much ethanol the fuel contains, as a percentage, on cars with a flex-fuel sensor. The ECU needs it because ethanol needs more fuel for the same air, so the whole fuelling strategy shifts with this number.

Vapour system pressure reported on an absolute scale rather than against the outside air. It carries the same information as the relative reading but never goes negative, which makes it easier to log across changing weather.
The wide-range version of the vapour pressure reading, covering a larger span than the fine-resolution one. Cars that run large-leak and small-leak tests report both, each suited to a different test.

Absolute fuel rail pressure, measured against vacuum rather than against the manifold. Direct injection systems report thousands of kPa here and vary it with load; a rail that cannot reach its target is a common cause of rough running under acceleration.
Accelerator pedal position expressed against the released position the ECU has learned, so it reads zero with your foot off. It is the pedal equivalent of the relative throttle figure.

How much useful life the hybrid battery pack has left, as a percentage, as the ECU estimates it. It is not the state of charge and it does not move as you drive; it is a slow health estimate that declines over years.

Engine oil temperature as the control unit reports it. Oil warms more slowly than coolant and settles higher, typically 90–110 °C in normal driving, and it is the better guide to whether the engine is truly warm. Sustained readings well past 120 °C shorten oil life.

The crank angle at which fuel injection is timed, in degrees. It matters on direct-injection and diesel engines, where moving injection earlier or later changes combustion noise, emissions and how much of the charge burns.

Fuel consumption in litres per hour, reported by the ECU itself rather than estimated. Where a car supports it, this is the more trustworthy of the two figures, because the ECU knows exactly how long it held the injectors open.

The torque the driver has asked for, as a percentage of the engine\'s reference torque. Multiply it by the reference figure to get newton metres. Compared with the delivered value it shows whether anything is limiting the engine.

The torque the engine is actually delivering, as a percentage of its reference torque. A persistent gap below the demanded figure means something is limiting output — knock control, a boost fault, or a deliberate protection strategy.

The engine\'s rated maximum torque in newton metres, which the percentage torque readings are scaled against. It is a fixed property of the engine, not a live measurement, so it does not change as you drive.

Mass of exhaust leaving the engine, in kilograms per hour. It follows air flow closely, since almost everything that goes in comes out, and aftertreatment strategies use it to work out how much they have to clean.

The gear ratio the gearbox reports — engine speed divided by output shaft speed — rather than the gear number on the dash. It is only meaningful while the car is moving: at a standstill the output shaft is not turning, so the ratio is undefined and the value parks at a placeholder.

Total distance the car has travelled, as the control unit holds it. Not every car exposes it, and where it does the figure should track the instrument cluster closely. It is the reading worth logging at the start and end of a trip.

Output voltage of a narrow-band oxygen sensor in the exhaust. It is a switch rather than a scale: around 0.1 V means lean, around 0.9 V means rich, and a healthy sensor before the catalyst swings between them several times a second. A sensor after the catalyst should instead sit fairly still around the middle, which is how a working converter shows itself.

The signal voltage from a wide-range oxygen sensor. It is not the 0.1–0.9 V switch a narrow-band sensor makes: a wideband probe reports its measurement as lambda, and this channel is the raw electrical signal behind it. Read the lambda channel for the mixture itself.

The fuel correction being applied on account of this particular oxygen sensor, in percent. It is the same idea as the bank fuel trim but attributed to one probe, which is what makes it useful on an engine with several sensors: it says which one the ECU is reacting to.

The mixture as a wide-range oxygen sensor actually measured it, where 1.000 is the chemically ideal air-fuel ratio. Below 1.000 is rich and above it is lean. Unlike the commanded value this is a measurement, so the difference between the two is the fuelling error the ECU has not corrected yet.

The pump current a wide-range oxygen sensor draws to hold its measuring cell at the reference mixture. It is how the sensor physically works rather than a reading to interpret directly — near zero means the exhaust is already at lambda 1, and the sign tells you which way it is off.

The instant fuel correction derived from the oxygen sensor behind the catalyst, in percent. The downstream sensor trims slowly and gently, because its job is to fine-tune what the upstream sensor is doing, not to control fuelling on its own. Large values here often accompany a tired converter.

The learned, stored correction derived from the oxygen sensor behind the catalyst. It drifts slowly over many drives and survives a restart, so a large stored value is a longer-standing story than the instant one — commonly an ageing converter or a lazy downstream sensor.

Mass of air entering the engine measured by one of the air flow sensors, in grams per second. Engines with two intake tracts report a sensor each; the pair should read closely together at the same load, and a persistent difference points at one sensor or one intake path.

Coolant temperature from one of the engine\'s coolant sensors. Cars with more than one measure at different points in the circuit, so the readings need not match exactly — the difference between them is what tells you about flow and thermostat behaviour.

Intake air temperature at one specific point in the intake tract, identified by bank and sensor number. Where a car reports several, the difference between the one nearest the inlet and the one nearest the engine is intake heat soak, which climbs when the car sits still and falls again on the move.

Temperature of the recirculated exhaust gas at one sensor position. It rises when the EGR valve is actually flowing, which makes it the practical check that recirculation is happening at all: a valve commanded open that produces no temperature rise is a valve that is not flowing.

Back pressure in the exhaust on one bank. It rises with engine load and with anything that restricts flow downstream, so a reading that climbs over time on a diesel usually means the particulate filter is loading up.

How fast the turbocharger shaft is spinning, in revolutions per minute. Turbos run in the tens of thousands of rpm and each has a limit the ECU protects; the figure is most interesting alongside boost pressure, since a turbo spinning hard without making pressure suggests a leak between it and the engine.

Temperature of the compressed intake air after the intercooler, at one sensor position. Compressing air heats it and the intercooler\'s whole job is to take that heat back out, so this reading is the direct measure of how well it is working — it climbs during sustained full throttle and falls again with airflow through the cooler.

Exhaust gas temperature at one sensor position, identified by bank and sensor number. These sensors protect the turbo and the aftertreatment from heat, and on a diesel they climb sharply during a particulate filter regeneration — which is the expected behaviour, not a fault.
